anchor: shall I not die like Enkidu
title: 'Shall I not die like Enkidu?'
short: The turning point: Gilgamish's grief becomes fear of his own death, and he sets out to find eternal life.
body: The fame he sought in Tablet III no longer satisfies; he wants life itself. The journey to Uta-Napishtim, the only mortal who gained immortality, fills Tablets IX-XI. The line moves the poem from the public world of heroic deeds to a private meditation on mortality. In George's edition the tablet begins with Gilgamish roaming the wild and asking this question aloud; he resolves to travel to Uta-Napishtim, the one human known to have escaped death, to learn his secret. The rest of the epic follows from this decision.

title: Uta-Napishtim, the Flood hero
short: Uta-Napishtim ('He found life') is the survivor of the Flood, made immortal by the gods: the Babylonian Noah.
body: Thompson's note: 'The Babylonian Noah'. In the Sumerian Flood story he is Ziusudra; in Atrahasis he is Atrahasis, 'Exceedingly Wise'. The name means 'he found life'. He lives 'far away', at the edge of the world. His father is Ubara-Tutu, king of Shuruppak before the Flood. He will tell his story in Tablet XI. Thompson writes the name with hyphens, as was the custom of his day; modern scholars write Uta-napishti or Utnapishtim.

title: Ubara-Tutu
short: Ubara-Tutu was king of Shuruppak before the Flood, father of Uta-Napishtim.
body: The Sumerian King List names Ubar-Tutu as the last antediluvian king, at Shuruppak. In the King List he reigned in Shuruppak, the last of the antediluvian kings, after which 'the Flood swept over'. Naming him as the father of Uta-Napishtim places the Flood hero in that royal line and in the city where the Flood story begins (XI). The patronymic is repeated by Ea when he addresses the hero through the reed wall: 'thou scion of Ubara-Tutu'.

title: The Moon-god (Sin)
short: Travelling at night among lions, Gilgamish prays to Sin, the Moon-god.
body: Sin, the Moon-god, was worshipped at Ur and Harran and lit the night roads. Gilgamish prays to him again in Tablet XII. His crescent shone on travellers at night, and he was regarded as a protector against the dangers of darkness. In George's text Gilgamish's prayer is followed by a dream, after which he attacks the lions he finds 'glorying in life'. Lions in the mountain passes were a real danger to travellers in the ancient Near East.

anchor: Mashu the name of the hills
title: Mount Mashu
short: Mashu ('twins') is the twin-peaked mountain where the sun rises and sets, with peaks reaching heaven and roots reaching the underworld.
body: Gilgamish passes through it by the sun's path: in George's text a tunnel of total darkness twelve double-hours long. The cosmic mountain links heaven, earth and the underworld. Thompson's note explains that the scorpion-men guard the sun 'at his rising and setting'. Gilgamish enters the mountain at sunset and must run through darkness before the sun overtakes him; in George's text the passage counts the double-hours one by one, with 'no light' at each, until he emerges into light at the end. The mythical geography places Mashu at the edge of the world, beyond which lies the ocean.

title: The scorpion-men
short: Scorpion-men guard the gate of the sun; one recognises Gilgamish as two-thirds divine.
body: Scorpion-men appear in Mesopotamian art and among Tiamat's monsters in Enuma Elish. Their glance is death and their terror overwhelming; Gilgamish turns pale at the sight of them. The scorpion-man and his wife discuss the stranger, recognise his divine part, and, after hearing his story, let him enter the mountain. Scorpion-men with human torsos and scorpion bodies are found on Babylonian boundary stones (kudurrus) and seals.

title: 'Two parts god'
short: The scorpion-man's wife repeats the formula of Tablet I.
body: Thompson used this passage to restore the formula in Tablet I. Her remark that a third of him is human hints that he will not escape death. The repetition reminds the reader that his mortal third is the problem he cannot solve. The dialogue of the two scorpion-beings, husband and wife, prefigures the later dialogue of Uta-Napishtim and his wife, who also discuss the visitor in Tablet XI.

title: The garden of jewels
short: At the end of the tunnel Gilgamish finds a garden of trees bearing jewels: carnelian fruit, lapis leaves.
body: Often compared with Eden as described in Ezekiel 28:13, where precious stones cover the 'garden of God'. In George's edition the trees bear carnelian and lapis lazuli and other gems, described one by one. The garden is the first sign that Gilgamish has reached the edge of the world, close to the realm of the gods and of the sun. Thompson's 'boskage' (thicket) and 'azure' are typical of his archaic diction. The beauty of the garden is static and lifeless: precious stones, not living fruit.

title: Shamash: 'You will not find the life you seek'
short: Shamash warns Gilgamish that the life he seeks he will not find; Gilgamish replies that he wants to see the sun.
body: These lines come from an Old Babylonian tablet (the 'Sippar' or Meissner tablet), not the standard version. The phrase recurs in Siduri's speech. Shamash's words anticipate those of Siduri, and both make the same point: the life Gilgamish seeks is not available to men. Thompson integrates the Old Babylonian lines into his Ninth Tablet; modern editions keep the versions separate, since the standard Babylonian poem does not contain this dialogue.

anchor: Let mine eyes see the Sun
title: Light and life
short: Gilgamish asks to see the sun: light is life, darkness death.
body: He has just crossed the darkness of Mashu. Having just emerged from the twelve double-hours of darkness inside Mount Mashu, the hero asks to be filled with sunlight; for a Mesopotamian, the dead 'see no light' (VII). The wish to look on the sun is a wish to remain among the living. Thompson's rendering, 'Let mine eyes see the Sun and be sated with brightness', gives the hexameter a Homeric ring.
